title: Shipped My First Game in 30 Days: Codex, Claude Code, and a Stack of Custom Tools
author: SeekingSpire
selftext:
[https://mythspire.itch.io/censorbreaker](https://mythspire.itch.io/censorbreaker) — free download, early playtest build.

Breakout meets Peggle — chain-reaction scoring across 24 levels (3 themes, 8 levels each) with instanced block rendering, 8 block types, 3 skill trees with ultimates, FMOD audio, real-time score popups via LitMotion, and a full TypeScript HUD through OneJS. Built in Unity 6.3 / 3D URP.

Started as a multi-mode prototype with an Arena mode that was cut during a hard pivot to a focused MVP. The AI workflow forced me to build custom tooling as production bottlenecks appeared. I think the tools I built around game development are probably more interesting than the game itself. Also, I'm not a programmer, so pretty much everything we built followed the pattern: “Can we MCP this?” followed by “Yes, we can.”

* **ComfyUI custom workflows** ("Donuts Delivery" JSON improved per theme by the agents) for anime-styled generations, tweaked for better prompt results from the Illustrious models used to generate the waifu art (Text2Image + Detailers).
* **FMOD MCP bridge (27 tools)** — agents create events, import audio, route buses, and build banks directly in FMOD Studio via TCP without touching the GUI.
* **Ableton MCP bridge (77 tools)** — programmatic music creation, MIDI editing, and stem export. Full Ableton Live Object Model access through a Remote Script + MCP server. *Note:* the music is a purchased asset. The SFX (block hits, explosions, bounces, etc.) were all created in Ableton, which I still have no clue how to use on my own.
* **OdinTools Deep Inspect** — custom Unity editor inspection scripts built on top of Coplay MCP. This allows AI to probe deeper than Coplay can on its own and made it possible to inspect and script completely visual editors like Behavior Designer Pro, enabling agents to build complex enemy behavior trees without me ever touching BDPro myself.
* **Glass Bridge** — a VS Code extension + MCP server that lets agents communicate across split terminals with full visibility. Claude Code and Codex share a governed workspace where one agent can observe and send commands to another agent’s terminal. All CLI interactions rely entirely on OAuth (no expensive API calls for GPT-5.4 / Opus-4.6).
* **Custom governance layer** hooked into Claude Code and shared with Codex via Glass Bridge. Two AI agents (Claude as lead, Codex as reviewer) collaborate under a formal task-packet protocol — dispatches, acknowledgments, completion handshakes, and evidence tagging.
* **Reverie** — an RLM-based memory retrieval system that indexes agent session transcripts across multiple agents. A root LM navigates session summaries, then loads and analyzes targeted sessions on demand. It sits alongside Project Memory MCP (40 tools), which uses ChromaDB and SQLite to track documentation, design decisions, and development lessons across projects. Git handles change control, but the memory systems give agents continuity across sessions.

The game itself is rough — it's an early playtest with bugs and not a lot of content yet. But the toolchain that came out of it is the real artifact. Every tool was built to solve a specific problem: agents couldn't hear what they were mixing, couldn't see Unity's inspector, couldn't talk to each other, and couldn't remember what happened yesterday.

I look forward to the next project yielding even more custom tooling and increasing in scope and complexity. I don’t think I’d be able to say I’ve ever “finished” a game before if it weren’t for these coding models.   
  
My agents also made me a decent looking little website [mythspire.com](http://mythspire.com)

comments.author: Apart_Athlete_8651
comments.body: Damn the custom tool list is impressive. I'm an audio guy making my own games now and I'm also using FMOD.

replies.author: SeekingSpire
replies.body:
I'm definitely not an audio guy even though I love music and wish I understood more about it. I do love what FMOD enabled for me.. Basically made multi-track SFX tied to a specific event something I can ask an agent to figure out after pointing at existing assets that I like or designing them with an agent in Ableton (both FMOD and Ableton would have taken me ages to figure out on my own)..  I also love how I can tweak every single track without digging through code/Unity editor (or without asking my agents to do so)..  
  
Curious to know what MCP tools might be helpful in FMOD for someone like yourself who probably already knows how to use it better than I ever will (by the way, the only reason I haven't shared the tools publicly is because I'm so new to all of this - I don't want to cause issues for people with incomplete/incorrect tooling that I'm mostly coming up with on the spot)...   
  
This is what my agents have come up with so far for FMOD:

FMOD MCP Server — Full Tool List (26 tools)  
  
Our FMOD MCP server connects AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) to a running FMOD Studio instance via its scripting API. Here's everything it can do:  
Project                                                                                                                                                                           - status — Check connection to FMOD Studio, return project info                                                                                                                   - save — Save the current project                                                                                                                                                 - build — Build all banks (compile events into .bank files for engine runtime)  
\- execute\_js — Execute arbitrary JavaScript in FMOD Studio's scripting engine (ES5). Escape hatch for anything the dedicated tools don't cover 

Events  
\- list\_events — List all events with name, path, and ID                                                                                                                           - create\_event — Create a new event with automatic folder hierarchy creation and bank assignment                                                                                  - get\_event — Get full details of an event by path                                                                                                                              - delete\_event — Delete an event by path, auto-cleans empty parent folders                                                                                                        

  Audio Import                                                                                                                                                                      - import\_audio — Import a WAV/OGG/FLAC file into the project's asset pool  
\- add\_sound — Import audio and add it as a SingleSound, MultiSound, or SoundScatterer instrument on a new track in an existing event                                                
\- create\_multi\_sound — Create an event with a MultiSound instrument from a folder of audio files (random variation pool)              
\- bulk\_import — Import all audio files from a folder as individual SingleSound instruments on separate tracks of an existing event                                                
\- search\_library — Keyword search across a 52K+ file audio library, returns results grouped by folder                                                                           

Banks                                                                                                                                                                           - list\_banks — List all banks in the project                                                                                                                                      - create\_bank — Create a new bank for organizing events into loadable groups                                                                                                    - assign\_to\_bank — Assign an event to a bank (required for builds)                                                                                                              

Mixer / Routing                                                                                                                                                                   - list\_buses — List all mixer buses with volume levels  
\- create\_bus — Create a mixer bus for volume control categories (SFX, Music, UI, etc.)                                                                                          - delete\_bus — Delete a mixer bus (events revert to Master output)                      
\- get\_event\_output — Get which bus an event's master track is routed to                                                                                                         - set\_event\_output — Route an event's master track to a specific bus                                                                                                            - get\_all\_event\_routing — Get the bus routing table for every event in the project                                                                                              - list\_snapshots — List all mixer snapshots (override sets for pause menu, underwater, etc.)                                                                                    - list\_vcas — List all VCAs (volume control aggregators for bus groups)                                                                                                           
Effects & Parameters                                                                                                                                                              - add\_effect — Add an audio effect to an event's master track (reverb, compressor, EQ, delay, chorus, distortion, flanger, limiter, pitch shifter, tremolo, highpass, lowpass, spatializer — 16 effect types)  
\- add\_parameter — Add a game parameter to an event for adaptive audio (continuous float or discrete enumeration labels)  
  
Unity Integration                                                                                                                                                                 - sync\_from\_csharp — Parse a Unity C# script for \[SerializeField\] EventReference fields, map them to FMOD event paths, and optionally create the missing events automatically. Keeps FMOD in sync with what your game code expects.

replies.author: Apart_Athlete_8651
replies.body: I'm really just learning FMOD myself as most of the games I've worked on used in-house tools but your agents seem to do most of the heavy lifting.  Could you tell them something like 'make all weapons the loudest sounds in the game' or 'duck all other audio when a character is speaking or a weapon is firing and bring them back up to their set levels when the dialog/sound ends?'

replies.author: SeekingSpire
replies.body:
(Claude Opus 4.6 1M Context Model > Agent "Ryn"):

Yes to both, but the reality is more interesting than just "tell the agent and it happens" — let me give you a concrete example.                                                                                                        
  
In Censorbreaker, chain reactions can trigger 8+ explosions within 50ms. The naive version was genuinely painful to listen to. An agent solved this by building a polyphony management system that works across both FMOD and game   code:     
  
On the FMOD side (via MCP tools): set up an SFX bus with a compressor (-3dB threshold, 2:1 ratio), a limiter, and reverb. Created separate buses for Music, SFX, and routed everything appropriately. The agent also set up parameter-driven events — my bounce sound has 9 variations selected by a bounce\_level parameter, fire sounds have 5 levels. All of that was created and configured through the MCP tools.

On the game code side (agent writing C#): hard-capped concurrent explosions at 3 instances with 120ms minimum spacing. During chain reactions, only every 3rd detonation actually plays. When more than 6 SFX are active globally, volume dynamically ducks — ramping from 100% down to 30% as you approach the 12-instance hard cap. During the victory cascade when everything shatters at once, it thins to every 4th sound at 60% volume.

So to your actual questions:

"Make all weapons the loudest" — An agent can absolutely do this. Create a Weapons bus, route all weapon events to it, set relative volumes. The MCP tools handle bus creation, event routing, and volume in one pass. The get\_all\_event\_routing tool lets it see the full routing table and make informed decisions about relative levels.

Ducking when speaking/firing — This is where it gets real. FMOD supports sidechain compression for exactly this, and an agent can set it up, but the dedicated MCP tools currently handle the structure (create bus, add compressor effect) while the fine-tuning (sidechain input routing, threshold/ratio tweaking) goes through an execute\_js escape hatch that sends raw JavaScript to FMOD Studio's scripting engine. What I found in practice is that the agent often builds something smarter than basic sidechain — like the dynamic ducking system above where it manages polyphony and volume in game code based on what's actually happening, rather than purely relying on FMOD's mixer to react.

The honest gap in the tools right now: I built them for the creation pipeline (events, sounds, buses, routing, effects, banks, builds, searching a 52K+ file audio library). The mixing/automation side (sidechain configuration, effect parameter tuning, snapshots, VCAs) is thinner — you can list what exists but creating/tweaking those requires execute\_js or doing it in FMOD Studio directly. For someone who actually knows mixing, that's probably the side you'd want better tooling for.

comments.author: Complex77
comments.body:
Very interesting! 
Did you create the OdinTools Deep Inspect yourself? 
How does it work? 
I'm currently struggling using behavior trees trying to have AI create interesting AIs

replies.author: SeekingSpire
replies.body:
Yes — my agents built it specifically to solve the exact problem of using AI to create better NPC AI (and more broadly to see inside of existing Unity Asset Store assets).

One clarification since the name can be misleading: **Odin Inspector isn’t actually what enables this.** I already had Odin Inspector in the project, and the goal of the tools was to “pierce into” opaque third-party asset data, so I called the suite **OdinTools**. But the mechanism that makes it work is really **CoPlay MCP + Unity editor scripts + C# reflection**.

The issue I ran into is that **Unity MCP servers are great at manipulating scenes but bad at inspecting complex third-party assets.**

I’m using Claude Code/Codex with **CoPlay MCP (\~86 Unity tools)**. It can create objects, modify components, edit prefabs, run play mode, etc. But it’s effectively blind to most asset internals.

Example with **Behavior Designer Pro**:

CoPlay can see the component and might show something like:

BehaviorTree  
tasks: count = 12

But it **cannot see what those 12 tasks actually are**.

That’s because the real tree data lives inside private serialized structures like:

\[SerializeField\] private BehaviorData m\_Data;

CoPlay only reads public properties. All the interesting data — tasks, hierarchy, variables — lives behind `[SerializeField] private` fields.

**The workaround was CoPlay’s** `execute_script` **tool.**

It lets the AI run arbitrary **C# inside the Unity editor process**. Once you're executing code inside the editor, you can use `System.Reflection` to access:

• private fields  
• nested serialized objects  
• vendor internal APIs  
• runtime state during play mode

So I built **OdinTools**, which is basically a suite of **13 editor inspection scripts** that serialize opaque asset structures into JSON the AI can read.

For **Behavior Designer**, the inspector does roughly this:

• accesses the private `m_Data` field  
• walks the internal task list  
• reconstructs parent/child relationships  
• reads `SharedVariable` bindings  
• outputs the complete tree hierarchy as JSON

There’s also a runtime inspector that can capture **which task is executing during Play Mode** via `BehaviorManager.instance`.

One important architectural choice: **no hard dependencies on vendor assemblies.**

Everything resolves dynamically using:

AppDomain.CurrentDomain.GetAssemblies()

If Behavior Designer (or any other asset) isn’t installed, the inspector just reports that the type wasn’t found instead of breaking the toolset. That also means the same inspection folder can drop into any Unity project.

If you're trying to have AI generate behavior trees, the real blocker is usually **visibility**.

If the AI cannot inspect the serialized tree structure, it’s essentially authoring blind.

Two approaches that tend to work well:

1. Write a small reflection inspector for your specific tree asset. Once the pattern is established, each new asset integration is relatively small.

2. Use a **code-first behavior tree library** (NPBehave). If the tree itself is C# code instead of serialized inspector data, the AI can read and generate it directly. (I haven't tested these yet myself but plan to adapt future projects away from visual editors so my agents aren't burning tokens fighting against them).

The hybrid approach is also powerful: design trees visually → extract the structure → have the AI reproduce or extend them in code.

Your comment/question inspired me to provide a better technical reference on my website:  
[Deep Inspect](https://mythspire.com/deep-inspect.html)

replies.author: SeekingSpire
replies.body:
Thanks for commenting. Out of curiosity, did any particular engine end up standing out to you as the most appealing—Unreal, Unity, Godot, or something custom?

I’m also curious how much of your traditional software development background has translated into game development for you. Do “good coding practices” map cleanly into game workflows, or do they end up looking different in practice?

From what I’ve seen so far, moving from prototype → system implementation seems to involve a lot of refactoring. I’m still trying to figure out whether that’s just normal for game development, or if it’s partly a side-effect of using agents that can be a bit sloppy with structure.

For example, I follow Unity Code Monkey and he seems to refactor pretty frequently, so it makes me think constant iteration might simply be part of the process.

Right now I’m trying to refine my spec → prototype → implement workflow. One thing I’m unsure about is how strict I should be early on about separating data from systems for easier management later. Another thing I’ve been experimenting with is periodically asking my agents things like: “Do we have any monolithic scripts that should be refactored?”—and surprisingly the answer is often yes every couple of days.

That makes me wonder whether I should enforce harder architectural rules up front, or if I’m just overthinking it. My current assumption is that smaller, focused scripts are better when working with agents since there’s less context to sift through and comments in each file can steer them more reliably. Curious if your experience lines up with that or if you’ve found a better approach.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body:
* **Glass Bridge** — a VS Code extension + MCP server that lets agents communicate across split terminals with full visibility. Claude Code and Codex share a governed workspace where one agent can observe and send commands to another agent’s terminal. All CLI interactions rely entirely on OAuth (no expensive API calls for GPT-5.4 / Opus-4.6). 

Have you tried Claude Code teams as well? Is this better or worse? Pros and cons?

replies.author: SeekingSpire
replies.body:
I haven’t tried it yet, but I plan to. My assumption is that native tooling for each agent will consistently be more reliable and evolve faster than anything custom-built. That said, I don’t see the “teams” feature as a replacement for Glass Bridge—more as a complementary extension.


The key difference is persistence and memory architecture. Glass Bridge logs agent activity into two separate systems: the Project Memory MCP and Reveries RLM. Together, these provide structured persistence with named identities across sessions, enabling tracking of effectiveness, changelogs, and long-term behavioral patterns.
In contrast, “teams” operates as a parallel swarm. Agents collaborate within a single session, exchange context, and then terminate. There’s no built-in persistence layer or identity continuity unless extended externally (e.g., via a custom MCP). It’s effectively a stateless, one-off collaborative execution model.


That swarm model is still useful. It allows large research or exploration tasks to run in parallel and then be consolidated into a single execution lane. However, it doesn’t replace the ongoing, cross-session collaboration I rely on—particularly between Claude and Codex.


That pairing has been the most effective in practice. Claude tends to be more creative and fluid, while Codex is stricter, governance-oriented, and often contrarian (especially 5.4). Their interaction surfaces gaps that single-agent outputs typically miss, producing more balanced and reliable results.
Long term, the goal is to leverage native features—teams, skills, CLI hooks—as modular extensions within the broader collaboration system built into VS Code. Each becomes a specialized capability rather than a replacement for the core architecture.


One of the main advantages of this approach is cost control: staying within subscription-based Oauth usage instead of scaling direct API calls, while remaining compliant with terms of service.
